title: Canary Readout — Mixed-Workload Scheduler (runtime-1.19 flag) — A/B vs baseline
content:
Redwood Inference — Serving Runtime
Canary Readout: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short/long prompt-aware policy)

Author: Omar El-Sayed
Reviewers: Sofia Ivanova (EM), Sean Gallagher (SRE), Jonas Weber (Perf), Rina Kobayashi (Bench harness)
Date window covered: 2025-01-14 through 2025-01-20 (inclusive)
Runtime build(s): runtime-1.19.0-rc2 → runtime-1.19.0-rc4
Flag: runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled (default OFF)
Policy: 2-queue short-first with fairness window + max-wait guardrails (see design/ADR)

Summary (executive)
- Outcome: Canary met the primary goal for latency-sensitive traffic under mixed prompt-length load.
- Result: p95 end-to-end latency for “short/interactive” class improved 18–27% in mixed workloads, while keeping overall throughput within the agreed regression budget.
- Stability: One canary regression was detected (queue depth growth under burst when long-prefill dominated and short queue was near-empty). This was mitigated by rc4 (backpressure thresholds by class + fix for priority inversion).
- Recommendation: GO for extended canary (wider slice) on Dedicated only, gated to specific routes, with current rollback triggers. Not recommended to expand to Hosted shared pools yet.

1) Canary goal and hypotheses
Goal (per project charter): Reduce p95 tail latency for latency-sensitive traffic when co-scheduled with long-context requests, without starving long prompts or materially regressing throughput.

Hypotheses
H1: Separating prefill-heavy requests prevents long-prefill from dominating dispatch, lowering short-class wait time and improving p95.
H2: Fairness guardrails keep long-class bounded (no starvation), even under sustained interactive load.
H3: Backpressure by class prevents overload from causing priority inversion and protects the short queue.

2) Rollout plan actually executed
2.1 Scope / where enabled
- Product surface: Redwood Dedicated clusters only (single-tenant), no API surface changes.
- Regions: us-east-1 (primary) and eu-west-1 (secondary) for validation.
- Models: “mid-size decoder-only” and “large decoder-only” in the Dedicated catalog (we avoided niche/experimental kernels).
- Traffic types included:
  - Streaming chat
  - Non-streaming text generation
  - Mixed context lengths (chat with RAG + summarization jobs)

2.2 Canary slice and timeline
- 2025-01-14 10:00–18:00 PT: perf-canary A/B in lab environment (synthetic + trace replay)
- 2025-01-15 09:30 PT: production canary start (0.5% of Dedicated capacity in us-east-1), route-pinned
- 2025-01-16: expanded to 1.0% us-east-1; added eu-west-1 at 0.5%
- 2025-01-17: paused expansion due to queue depth anomaly during burst window (see Incident/Findings)
- 2025-01-18: rolled forward to rc4 with fixes; resumed at 1.0% us-east-1, 0.5% eu-west-1
- 2025-01-20: held steady; captured full weekday cycle; prepared this readout

2.3 Configuration and safety rails
- Flag scope: per-cluster override only; default remains OFF globally.
- Kill switch: runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled can be disabled within ~2 minutes via config propagation.
- Additional runtime safety:
  - Max-wait bound for long-class (guardrail to force service)
  - Periodic long-queue service even when short queue is non-empty
  - Separate admission control thresholds per class (introduced in rc4)

3) Dashboards and what we watched
Primary canary dashboards (pinned during on-call)
- Mixed-workload scheduler overview:
  - https://dash.redwood.ai/d/serving-runtime/mixed-workload-scheduler-overview
- Tail latency breakdown (p95/p99) by class + route:
  - https://dash.redwood.ai/d/serving-runtime/latency-tail-breakdown-by-class
- Queueing health:
  - https://dash.redwood.ai/d/serving-runtime/queue-depth-wait-time-by-class
- Starvation guardrails:
  - https://dash.redwood.ai/d/serving-runtime/starvation-guardrails

Key signals (high-level)
- Latency: end-to-end p50/p95/p99, plus “time-to-first-token” (TTFT) for streaming.
- Queueing: queue depth, enqueue→dequeue wait time histograms per class.
- Service split: prefill vs decode time breakdown.
- Throughput/cost: tokens/sec per GPU, GPU utilization, batch sizes.
- Reliability: error rate, timeouts, retries, 5xx, shed events.

4) Results (A/B: baseline vs scheduler ON)
Note: Numbers below are aggregated across canary slice only; not global fleet. We primarily compared “scheduler ON” vs a pinned baseline config on the same hardware/cluster class. Where possible we used the perf-canary A/B harness summary to reduce confounders.

4.1 Mixed workload scenarios (production canary)
Short/interactive class (primary success metric)
- TTFT p95: improved 19–25% (largest gains during overlapping long-prefill windows)
- End-to-end p95 latency: improved 18–27%
- End-to-end p99 latency: improved 10–18% (more variance, still positive)

Long/prefill-heavy class (fairness / no-starvation)
- End-to-end p95 latency: +0–6% (small regression in some windows, expected due to prioritization)
- Max observed wait time: remained below guardrail threshold after rc4
- Starvation events: 0 after rc4 (see definition below)

Overall throughput and utilization (regression budget)
- Tokens/sec per GPU: -0.8% to -2.4% depending on cluster and model
- GPU utilization: flat to slightly down (-0–1.5%), consistent with reduced batching opportunities when short traffic is heavy
- Decode batch sizes: slightly smaller median batch during peak interactive windows (expected)

4.2 Perf-canary (lab) confirmation
Lab replay aligned with prod directionally.
- Synthetic 70/30 mix (short/long arrivals) showed consistent short-class p95 improvements (20%+)
- Trace replay “summarization burst + chat steady” scenario showed reduced short wait-time tail, but identified the priority inversion bug fixed in pr_8468.

5) Regressions, anomalies, and what we changed
5.1 Incident: queue depth growth during burst (2025-01-17)
Symptom
- In us-east-1 canary slice, the long queue depth trended upward for ~35 minutes during a customer burst window. p95 short latency still improved, but backlog growth was visible and SRE asked to pause expansion.

Impact
- No customer-facing outage; a small increase in long-class completion time was observed.
- Risk: sustained backlog could have crossed into timeout territory if the burst continued.

Root cause (most likely)
- Admission control was shared across classes, and long-prefill arrivals could occupy capacity in a way that delayed long-queue drain after short-queue fluctuations.
- Additionally, we confirmed a priority inversion edge case: short requests could be blocked behind an in-flight long-prefill batch under specific batching timing.

Mitigation / fix
- Applied rc4 with:
  - Separate admission control thresholds by class (redwood/pr_8462)
  - Priority inversion regression fix + test (redwood/pr_8468)
- Post-fix: backlog behavior stabilized; long queue depth returned to pre-canary baseline patterns under similar bursts.

5.2 Metrics / observability gaps
- We initially lacked a single “starvation event counter” with a crisp definition. We added a derived alert condition in the dashboard based on max-wait histogram quantiles and a sampled structured log query.
- Action item: promote starvation metrics to first-class counters in runtime (tracked in ENG-4831 follow-up; not blocking this canary recommendation).

6) Definitions used (so we don’t argue later)
Classification
- Short vs long classification is based on prompt tokens and predicted prefill cost (classifier introduced earlier; canary used conservative thresholding).
- Streaming vs non-streaming is not a class by itself; it is a dimension we slice by in dashboards.

Starvation (operational)
- A “starvation event” is counted operationally if any long-class request exceeds max_wait_ms_long bound OR if the starvation guardrail forces service repeatedly while long queue depth continues to grow.
- In this canary, we treat any sustained period (>10 minutes) of long max-wait p99 exceeding the bound as a rollback candidate.

7) Go/No-Go recommendation
Recommendation: GO — extend canary scope on Dedicated (not Hosted) with tight guardrails.

Rationale
- Primary objective achieved: meaningful p95 improvements for latency-sensitive traffic under mixed workloads.
- Throughput regression remained within the agreed budget (<= ~3% observed, typically <2.5%).
- The only meaningful instability observed was addressed with rc4, and subsequent windows did not reproduce the backlog growth.

Proposed next step (extended canary)
- Expand to 5% of Dedicated capacity in us-east-1 for 72 hours.
- Keep eu-west-1 at 1% as a “signal region” for regression detection.
- Scope to routes known to have mixed workloads (chat + summarization overlap) rather than blanket enabling.
- Continue default-OFF for Hosted + shared pools until we validate interactions with noisier neighbors and more heterogeneous kernels.

Approvals requested
- Serving Runtime: Sofia Ivanova
- SRE: Sean Gallagher (or delegate)
- Perf program: Jonas Weber
- Product (rollout): Paula Mendes

8) Rollback criteria (hard triggers)
If any trigger occurs, disable the flag in the affected cluster(s) immediately, then escalate in #eng-runtime and #eng-sre.

A) Latency regressions
- Short/interactive end-to-end p95 worsens by >10% vs baseline for 15+ minutes, on any canary cluster
- TTFT p95 worsens by >10% vs baseline for 15+ minutes (streaming routes)
- Any sustained p99 blow-up (>20% vs baseline for 10+ minutes) with correlated queue wait time increase

B) Starvation / fairness
- Long-class max-wait p99 exceeds the configured bound for >10 minutes
- Long queue depth monotonically increases for >20 minutes AND long-class completion time p95 degrades >15%

C) Reliability / errors
- 5xx rate increases by >0.2% absolute vs baseline for 10+ minutes
- Timeout rate increases by >0.1% absolute vs baseline for 10+ minutes
- Admission control shedding increases and correlates with customer-visible failures (not just protective shedding)

D) Capacity / throughput
- Tokens/sec per GPU degrades by >5% sustained for >30 minutes (outside known peak interactive windows)
- GPU utilization drops >5% sustained without corresponding latency wins (suggests mis-batching or scheduler overhead)

Operational rollback steps
1) Flip runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled = false for the canary cluster(s)
2) Confirm within ~5 minutes that queue depth and latency revert toward baseline
3) Capture a 15-minute window of scheduler logs (sampled) and export the dashboard snapshot
4) File an incident note if customer impact occurred; otherwise log as canary issue

9) Open questions / follow-ups (not blocking extended canary)
- Classifier tuning:
  - Can we reduce misclassification under unusual tokenization patterns (very long system prompts, tool schemas)?
  - Evaluate EWMA-based refinement (planned work; see later PRs in project notes).
- Scheduling parameters:
  - Fairness window defaults: validate across a wider range of arrival processes (bursty vs smooth).
  - Confirm stability under extreme long-only bursts followed by interactive spikes (oscillation risk).
- Observability:
  - Add explicit starvation counters and “forced long service” counters in runtime exports.
  - Standardize metric names to match the dashboard pack (avoid drift).

10) Appendix: quick notes for reviewers
What changed between rc2 and rc4?
- rc2: baseline two-queue policy + basic guardrails
- rc3: metrics improvements + initial backpressure work
- rc4: separate admission control thresholds by class + priority inversion fix + regression test

Where to find raw evidence
- perf-canary summary output: https://perf-canary.redwood.ai/runs?tag=mixed-workload-scheduler-rc4
- dashboard snapshots folder: https://drive.redwood.ai/shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/canary-snapshots/2025-01-mixed-workload-scheduler
- incident thread: Slack incidents/thread_1731462200_900114

Contact
